workEn: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi
title: Branwen uerch Lyr
titleEn: Branwen, Daughter of Llŷr — Branwen's starling and the house in Ireland
part: Branwen's starling and the house in Ireland
source: Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi, Second Branch, from the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth 4, c. 1350) as printed in J. Gwenogvryn Evans, The White Book Mabinogion (Pwllheli, 1907), columns 47–55; public domain. Readings are the manuscript's as Evans prints them, checked against the page images; word division, punctuation, capitals and quotation marks are ours. Where the White Book omits a word the sense requires, it is supplied from the Red Book (Rhŷs & Evans) and the note says so. Pronunciation convention: the manuscript spelling read with the sounds of Welsh c. 1300. Translations made fresh from the Welsh.

sentences.t: Dilit ymdidan a wnaethant y nos honno, tra uu da ganthunt, a cherd a chyuedach.
sentences.l: Pursuing conversation they-did that night, while it-was good with-them, and song and carousing.
sentences.i: They kept up the talk that night for as long as it pleased them, with song and carousing.
sentences.n: Dilit ymdidan a wnaethant 'pursuing talk they did': a verbal noun (dilit, from dilyn 'follow') closed by a wnaethant 'they did', the narrative pattern for a plain 'they kept up talk'. The part opens mid-line in Evans col. 47, straight after the cauldron story, with no large initial. tra uu da ganthunt 'while it was good with them': uu ← bu, preterite of bot, softened after tra 'while'. a cherd ← kerd 'song, music' and a chyuedach ← kyuedach 'carousing', both with the spirant mutation after a 'and'.

sentences.t: A phan welsant uot yn llessach udunt uynet y gyscu noc eisted a wei hwy, y gyscu yd aethant.
sentences.l: And when they-saw being more-profitable for-them going to sleep than sitting that-would-be longer, to sleep they-went.
sentences.i: And when they saw that it would profit them more to go to sleep than to sit any longer, they went to bed.
sentences.n: uot ← bot 'being', softened as the object of welsant 'they saw'. llessach is the comparative of lles 'benefit': 'more profitable'. udunt 'for them' (y conjugated). noc 'than' (no with c before a vowel). a wei hwy 'that would be longer': wei is bei, the imperfect subjunctive of bot, softened after a, the v-sound written w here where the scribe usually writes u; hwy 'longer', comparative of hir. y gyscu yd aethant 'to sleep they went': the adverbial phrase first, so the verb takes yd — the same close as the feast in the last part.

sentences.t: Ac yuelly y treulyssant y wled honno drwy digriuwch.
sentences.l: And thus they-spent that feast through amusement.
sentences.i: And so they passed that feast in pleasure.
sentences.n: yuelly 'thus'. treulyssant 'they spent', 3 pl. preterite (-yssant) of treulaw 'spend, pass (time)'; ss is simply s. y wled ← gwled 'feast', softened after the article because it is feminine. digriuwch 'amusement' (digrifwch; u = v).

sentences.t: Ac yn niwed hynny, y kychwynnwys Matholwch, a Branuen y gyt ac ef, parth ac Iwerdon.
sentences.l: And in the end of that, set-out Matholwch, and Branwen together with him, towards Ireland.
sentences.i: And at the end of it Matholwch set out for Ireland, and Branwen with him.
sentences.n: yn niwed hynny 'in the end of that': diwed 'end' with the nasal mutation after yn 'in' (d > n). y kychwynnwys 'set out': the verb comes first after the particle y, and -wys is the old 3 sg. preterite ending. Branuen is the same name as Branwen, the w written u. y gyt ac ef 'together with him'; parth ac 'towards'.

sentences.t: A hynny o Abermenei y kychwynnyssant teir llong ar dec, ac y doethant hyt yn Iwerdon.
sentences.l: And that, from Aber Menai they-set-out, three ships on ten, and they-came as-far-as into Ireland.
sentences.i: They set out from Aber Menai, thirteen ships, and came to Ireland.
sentences.n: A hynny 'and that' is a loose connective in this tale, roughly 'and so'. Abermenei is Aber Menai, the mouth of the Menai strait. kychwynnyssant is 3 pl. preterite (-yssant); since a noun subject after its verb normally takes a singular verb, teir llong ar dec 'three ships on ten' = thirteen is better taken in apposition, 'they set out, thirteen ships'. hyt yn 'as far as into'.

sentences.t: Yn Iwerdon, dirwawr lywenyd a uu wrthunt.
sentences.l: In Ireland, huge gladness it-was-that was towards-them.
sentences.i: In Ireland there was great rejoicing at their coming.
sentences.n: dirwawr 'huge' (dir- + mawr, softened in the compound; the last part has diruawr). lywenyd ← llywenyd 'joy', softened after the adjective set before it. a uu 'was': uu ← bu, softened after a — the subject first, then a and the verb, the abnormal sentence. wrthunt 'towards them' (wrth conjugated): joy 'towards' guests is a welcome.

sentences.t: Ny doey wr mawr, na gwreic da yn Iwerdon, e ymwlet a Branwen, ni rodei hi ae cae ae modrwy ae teyrndlws cadwedic ydaw, a uei arbennic y welet yn mynet e ymdeith.
sentences.l: There-would-not-come a-great man, nor a-good woman in Ireland, to visit with Branwen, that-not she-would-give either a-brooch or a-ring or a-kingly-jewel treasured to-him, that would-be notable to see going away.
sentences.i: No great man or good woman in Ireland came to visit Branwen but she gave them a brooch, or a ring, or a treasured jewel fit for a king, which made a fine show as they went away.
sentences.n: Ny doey 'there did not come': doey is the imperfect of dyuot, habitual 'would come'. wr ← gwr, the subject softened straight after the verb. e ymwlet 'to visit': e is a spelling of y 'to' (Evans prints e ymwlet; the second witness's ymw[e]let is not adopted). ni rodei hi 'that she did not give': two negatives, 'none came that she did not give', so everyone was given something. ae … ae … ae 'either … or … or'. cae 'brooch, clasp' (GPC also 'band, necklace'). teyrndlws looks like teyrn 'monarch' + tlws 'jewel' (t softened to d in the compound), 'a kingly jewel'; it is a rare word and its exact sense is uncertain. cadwedic 'kept, treasured'. ydaw is idaw 'to him'. a uei arbennic y welet 'that would be notable to see': uei, imperfect subjunctive of bot. e ymdeith 'away'.

sentences.t: Ac ymysc hynny, y ulwydyn honno a duc hi yn glotuawr, a hwyl delediw a duc hi o glot a chedymdeithon.
sentences.l: And amidst that, that year it-was-that she-bore renownedly, and a-comely course it-was-that she-bore of fame and of-companions.
sentences.i: And so she passed that year in great renown, and fared handsomely in fame and in friends.
sentences.n: y ulwydyn honno 'that year': blwydyn softened after the article (feminine), put first as the object. a duc hi 'she bore': duc, preterite of dwyn 'carry', here 'spend (time)'. yn glotuawr 'renownedly': clot 'fame' + mawr, softened after adverbial yn. hwyl 'course, fortune' (how things go); delediw ← telediw 'comely, seemly', softened after the feminine hwyl. o glot ← clot after o; a chedymdeithon ← kedymdeithon 'companions', spirant after a.

sentences.t: Ac yn hynny, beichogi a damweinwys idi y gael.
sentences.l: And meanwhile, pregnancy it-was-that befell to-her, its getting.
sentences.i: And meanwhile it befell her to conceive.
sentences.n: yn hynny 'meanwhile'. beichogi 'pregnancy' is the subject, put first. damweinwys 'befell', -wys preterite of damweinyaw. idi 'to her' (y conjugated, feminine). y gael 'its getting', i.e. to get it: y 'its' (beichogi) softens kael.

sentences.t: A guedy treulaw yr amseroyd dylyedus, mab a anet idi.
sentences.l: And after spending the times due, a-son it-was-that was-born to-her.
sentences.i: And when the due time had run its course, a son was born to her.
sentences.n: guedy 'after' (gu for gw). treulaw 'spending'. amseroyd 'times', plural of amser (-oyd = -oedd). dylyedus 'due, rightful', from dylyu 'owe, be entitled'. a anet 'was born': ganet, impersonal preterite of geni, softened after a, the g dropping away.

sentences.t: Sef enw a dodet ar y mab, Guern uab Matholwch.
sentences.l: That-is the name that was-put on the boy, Gwern son of-Matholwch.
sentences.i: The name given to the boy was Gwern son of Matholwch.
sentences.n: Sef enw a dodet 'that is the name that was put', and the answer follows: sef names it. dodet, impersonal preterite of dodi 'put'; to put a name on someone is to name him. Guern is Gwern (gu for gw), 'alder'. Evans prints uab here (the second witness ab); uab ← mab, softened after a name.

sentences.t: Rodi y mab ar uaeth a wnaethpwyt ar un lle goreu y wyr yn Iwerdon.
sentences.l: Giving the boy to fosterage it-was-that was-done, on the one place best for men in Ireland.
sentences.i: The boy was put out to be fostered in the very best place in Ireland for men.
sentences.n: Rodi … a wnaethpwyt 'giving … was done': the verbal-noun pattern with the impersonal of gwneuthur; wnaethpwyt ← gwnaethpwyt, softened after a. ar uaeth ← maeth 'nurture': 'to fosterage', the noble custom of rearing a child in another household. un lle goreu 'the one best place' (it could also mean 'one of the best places'). y wyr ← gwyr 'men', softened after y 'of, for'.

sentences.t: A hynny yn yr eil ulwydyn, llyma ymodwrd yn Iwerdon am y guaradwyd a gawssei Matholwch yg Kymry, a'r somm a wnathoedit idaw am y ueirch.
sentences.l: And that in the second year, behold a-murmuring in Ireland about the disgrace that Matholwch had-got in Wales, and the trick that had-been-done to-him about his horses.
sentences.i: Then in the second year a murmuring arose in Ireland over the insult Matholwch had suffered in Wales and the trick played on him over his horses.
sentences.n: eil 'second' softens: eil ulwydyn ← blwydyn. llyma 'behold' sets a scene with a bare noun. ymodwrd: a rare word, apparently 'stir, murmuring, commotion'; the sense is uncertain. a gawssei 'had got': cawssei, the pluperfect (-ssei) of kaffael, softened after a. yg Kymry 'in Wales': yn + Kymry, nasal mutation, written yg K. somm 'trick, deceit'. a wnathoedit 'that had been done': a pluperfect impersonal (-oedit) of gwneuthur. y ueirch ← meirch 'his horses', softened after y 'his'.

sentences.t: A hynny y urodyr maeth, a'r gwyr nessaf gantaw, yn lliwaw idaw hynny, a heb y gelu.
sentences.l: And that, his foster-brothers, and the men nearest with-him, reproaching to-him that, and without its hiding.
sentences.i: His foster-brothers and the men closest to him threw it in his face, and made no secret of it.
sentences.n: The sentence has no finite verb: a subject and then yn + verbal noun, 'were reproaching'. y urodyr maeth ← brodyr 'his foster-brothers', softened after y 'his'. nessaf 'nearest'. gantaw 'with him'. lliwaw 'colour' also means 'cast up against, taunt'; idaw 'to him'. heb y gelu 'without its hiding': y 'its' softens kelu.

sentences.t: A nachaf y dygyuor yn Iwerdon hyt nat oed lonyd idaw ony chaei dial y sarahet.
sentences.l: And behold the uproar in Ireland, so-that there-was-not quiet to-him unless he-should-get vengeance (for) his insult.
sentences.i: And such an uproar arose in Ireland that he could have no peace unless he took vengeance for the insult.
sentences.n: nachaf 'behold'. y dygyuor 'the uprising, uproar'. hyt nat 'so that not'. lonyd ← llonyd 'quiet', softened after oed (Evans's asterisk after lonyd is dropped). ony chaei 'unless he got': ony 'if not' gives the spirant to kaei, the imperfect subjunctive of kaffael. sarahet (sarhaed) is both the insult and the legal fine owed for it.

sentences.t: Sef dial a wnaethant, gyrru Branwen o un ystauell ac ef, a'y chymell y bobi yn y llys, a pheri y'r kygyd, gwedy bei yn dryllyaw kic, dyuot idi a tharaw bonclust arnei beunyd.
sentences.l: That-is the vengeance they-did: driving Branwen from one chamber with him, and her compelling to bake in the court, and causing to the butcher, after he-would-be cutting-up meat, to-come to-her and strike a-box-on-the-ear on-her daily.
sentences.i: The vengeance they took was to drive Branwen out of the chamber she shared with him, and make her bake in the court, and have the butcher, when he had been cutting up meat, come to her every day and box her ear.
sentences.n: Sef dial a wnaethant 'that is the vengeance they did', then a string of verbal nouns tells what it was. o un ystauell ac ef 'from (sharing) one chamber with him'. a'y chymell 'and her compelling': 'y 'her' gives the spirant, kymell > chymell. y bobi ← pobi 'to bake'. y'r kygyd 'to the butcher'. gwedy bei 'after he would be': bei, imperfect subjunctive of bot. a tharaw ← taraw 'strike', spirant after a. bonclust 'a box on the ear' (bon 'base' + clust 'ear'). beunyd 'daily' (pob + dyd).

sentences.t: Ac yuelly y gwnaethpwyt y foen.
sentences.l: And thus was-done her punishment.
sentences.i: And so her punishment was carried out.
sentences.n: gwnaethpwyt, impersonal preterite of gwneuthur. y foen 'her punishment': poen with the spirant after y 'her' (p > ph), the ph written f, as in A frynhawngueith in the last part.

sentences.t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb y wyr wrth Uatholwch, “par weithon wahard y llongeu, a'r yscraffeu, a'r corygeu, ual nat el neb y Gymry; ac a del yma o Gymry, carchara wynt ua na at trachefyn, rac gwybot hynn.”
sentences.l: “Yes, Lord,” said his men to Matholwch, “cause now forbidding the ships, and the ferry-boats, and the coracles, so-that not may-go anyone to Wales; and what may-come here from Wales, imprison them, [ua] do-not-let back, lest knowing this.”
sentences.i: “Yes, Lord,” his men said to Matholwch, “now have the ships and the ferry-boats and the coracles stopped, so that no one may go to Wales; and whoever comes here from Wales, imprison them and do not let them go back, so that this may not be known.”
sentences.n: heb y wyr ← gwyr 'his men'; wrth Uatholwch ← Matholwch, softened after wrth (Evans prints this line in a condensed size). par 'cause', imperative of peri; weithon 'now'; wahard ← gwahard 'forbid', softened. yscraffeu 'ferry-boats' (ysgraff); corygeu 'coracles'. nat el 'may not go': el, present subjunctive of mynet. a del 'whoever may come'. carchara 'imprison', imperative. ua na at trachefyn is uncertain: ua is certain on the page, the second witness puts [ac] in its place, and the Red Book reads hyt nat elont dracheuyn 'so that they may not go back'. It is read here as 'and do not let (them) back' — na at, negative imperative of gadu 'let' (at ← gat, softened after na, the g dropping away) — with ua perhaps a slip for a/ac, but the reading is not sure. trachefyn 'back'. rac gwybot hynn 'lest this be known'.

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny y diskynyssant.
sentences.l: And on that they-settled.
sentences.i: And on that they agreed.
sentences.n: diskynyssant 'they settled', 3 pl. preterite of diskynnu 'come down, alight', here 'come down on' a course, as A disgynnu a wnaeth ar gymryt hynny in the last part.

sentences.t: Blwynyded nit llei no their y buant yuelly.
sentences.l: Years not less than three they-were thus.
sentences.i: Not less than three years they went on so.
sentences.n: Blwynyded 'years', a plural of blwydyn. nit llei no their 'not less than three': llei 'less'; no 'than' gives the spirant to teir (feminine 'three'), written their. With this put first, the verb takes y: y buant 'they were', 3 pl. preterite of bot.

sentences.t: Ac yn hynny, meithryn ederyn drydwen a wnaeth hitheu ar dal y noe gyt a hi, a dyscu ieith idi, a menegi y'r ederyn y ryw wr oed y brawt.
sentences.l: And meanwhile, rearing a-bird starling she-did she-for-her-part on the edge of her kneading-trough with her, and teaching speech to-her, and telling to the bird the kind of man was her brother.
sentences.i: And meanwhile she reared a starling on the edge of her kneading-trough beside her, and taught it speech, and told the bird what manner of man her brother was.
sentences.n: meithryn … a wnaeth hitheu 'rearing she did, she for her part'. ederyn drydwen 'a starling bird': drydwen is taken as drudwen, the feminine singular of drudwy 'starling'; it is a rare form and the identification is not certain. The bird is feminine in what follows (idi, y phluf). ar dal y noe 'on the end of her kneading-trough': tal 'end, front' softened after ar. ieith 'speech, language'. y'r ederyn 'to the bird'. y ryw wr 'the kind of man': rhyw softened after the article, gwr after ryw.

sentences.t: A dwyn llythyr y poeneu a'r amharch a oed arnei hitheu.
sentences.l: And bringing a-letter of the pains and the dishonour that was on-her she-for-her-part.
sentences.i: And she made a letter of the sufferings and the dishonour that she was under.
sentences.n: dwyn 'bring, carry', here with llythyr 'letter': to produce or set down a letter; the verbal-noun narrative continues with Branwen as the understood subject. poeneu 'pains', plural of poen. amharch 'dishonour' (am- + parch 'respect'). arnei 'on her'.

sentences.t: A'r llythyr a rwymwyt am uon eskyll yr ederyn, a'y anuon parth a Chymry, a'r ederyn a doeth y'r ynys honn.
sentences.l: And the letter was-bound about the root of the wings of the bird, and its sending towards Wales, and the bird it-was-that came to this island.
sentences.i: And the letter was tied about the roots of the bird's wings, and it was sent off towards Wales, and the bird came to this island.
sentences.n: a rwymwyt ← rhwymwyt, impersonal preterite of rhwymaw 'bind', softened after a. uon ← bon 'base, root', softened after am. eskyll 'wings', plural of asgell. a'y anuon 'and its sending'. a Chymry ← Kymry, spirant after a 'to'. y'r ynys honn 'to this island', Britain, where the tale is told.

sentences.t: Sef lle y cauas Uendigeiduran, yg Kaer Seint yn Aruon, yn dadleu idaw dydgweith.
sentences.l: That-is the place it-found Bendigeidfran, at Caer Seint in Arfon, holding-pleas to-him one-day.
sentences.i: It found Bendigeidfran at Caer Seint in Arfon, where he was holding court one day.
sentences.n: Sef lle y cauas 'that is the place where it found': cauas, preterite of kaffael 'get, find', with the bird as subject; Uendigeiduran ← Bendigeiduran is softened as the object. yg Kaer Seint 'at Caer Seint' (by Caernarfon): yn + K, written yg K. Aruon 'Arfon'. yn dadleu 'pleading', holding a court of law; idaw 'to him' is loose here, like yn llys idaw 'at a court of his' in the last part. dydgweith 'one day'.

sentences.t: A diskynnu ar e yscwyd, a garwhau y phluf, yny arganuuwyt y llythyr, ac adnabot meithryn yr ederyn yg kyuanned.
sentences.l: And alighting on his shoulder, and roughening her feathers, until was-noticed the letter, and recognising the rearing of the bird in a-dwelling.
sentences.i: And it alighted on his shoulder and ruffled its feathers until the letter was seen, and it was plain that the bird had been reared among people.
sentences.n: diskynnu 'alighting', with the bird as subject. ar e yscwyd 'on his shoulder': e = y 'his'. garwhau 'roughening' (garw 'rough' + -hau): ruffling. y phluf 'her feathers': pluf with the spirant after y 'her'. yny 'until'. arganuuwyt, impersonal preterite of arganuot 'catch sight of'. adnabot 'recognise'. yg kyuanned 'in a dwelling, among people': yn + kyuanned 'inhabited place'.

sentences.t: Ac yna kymryt y llythyr a'y edrych.
sentences.l: And then taking the letter and its looking-at.
sentences.i: And then he took the letter and looked at it.
sentences.n: Two verbal nouns serve as the verbs, with Bendigeidfran understood as subject. a'y edrych 'and its looking at': 'y 'its'.

sentences.t: A phan darllewyt y llythyr, doluryaw a wnaeth o glybot y poen oed ar Uranwen, a dechreu o'r lle hwnnw peri anuon kennadeu y dygyuoryaw yr ynys honn y gyt.
sentences.l: And when was-read the letter, grieving he-did from hearing the pain that-was on Branwen, and beginning from that place causing sending messengers to muster this island together.
sentences.i: And when the letter was read, he grieved to hear of the suffering that was upon Branwen, and from that very place he began to have messengers sent to muster this island.
sentences.n: darllewyt 'was read', impersonal preterite of darllein. doluryaw a wnaeth 'grieving he did' (dolur 'pain, grief'). o glybot ← clybot 'hearing', softened after o. y poen oed 'the pain (that) was', a relative without a. ar Uranwen ← Branwen, softened after ar. peri anuon 'causing to send'. dygyuoryaw 'muster, raise a host'.

sentences.t: Ac yna y peris ef dyuot llwyr wys pedeir degwlat a seithugeint hyt attaw, ac e hun cwynaw wrth hynny, bot y poen a oed ar y chwaer.
sentences.l: And then he-caused he the coming of the full summons of-four ten-lands and seven-score to-him, and he himself complaining to that (host), the being of the pain that was on his sister.
sentences.i: And then he had the full levy of the seven score and fourteen lands come to him, and he himself made complaint to them of the suffering his sister was under.
sentences.n: y peris ef 'he caused', 3 sg. preterite of peri. llwyr wys 'full summons': gwys 'summons, levy', softened after llwyr set before it. pedeir degwlat a seithugeint reads literally 'four ten-lands and seven score' (wlat ← gwlat, softened in the compound degwlat); it is most easily taken as pedeir ar dec gwlat 'fourteen lands' + seith ugeint 'seven score', i.e. 154, the count of all the lands under Bendigeidfran. The Red Book has no deg: pedeir gwlat a seith ugeint 'four lands and seven score', i.e. 144. The White Book is kept and its reckoning is not certain. e hun 'himself'. cwynaw wrth 'complain to'. bot y poen 'that the pain was': bot gives the content of the complaint.

sentences.t: Ac yna kymryt kynghor.
sentences.l: And then taking counsel.
sentences.i: And then counsel was taken.
sentences.n: A bare verbal noun as the sentence's verb, as Yn y lle trannoeth, kymryt kynghor in the last part; kynghor is both 'counsel' and 'council'.

sentences.t: Sef kynghor a gahat, kyrchu Iwerdon, ac adaw seithwyr y dywyssogyon yma, a Chradawc uab Bran y benhaf, ac eu seith marchawc.
sentences.l: That-is the counsel that was-got: making-for Ireland, and leaving seven-men as princes here, and Caradog son of-Brân as their chief, and their seven horsemen.
sentences.i: The counsel they reached was to make for Ireland, and to leave seven men here as princes, with Caradog son of Brân as their chief, and their seven horsemen.
sentences.n: Sef kynghor a gahat 'that is the counsel that was got': gahat ← cahat, impersonal preterite of kaffael, softened after a, as Sef a gahat yn y kynghor in the last part. seithwyr 'seven men' (seith + gwyr). y dywyssogyon ← tywyssogyon 'princes' and y benhaf ← pennaf 'chief', each softened after y 'as'. a Chradawc ← Cradawc, spirant after a: Caradog. Bran is Brân, Bendigeidfran himself (bendigeit 'blessed' + bran). seith marchawc 'seven horsemen': the noun stays singular after a numeral.

sentences.t: Yn Edeirnon yd edewit y gwyr hynny, ac o achaws hynny y dodet Seith Marchawc ar y dref.
sentences.l: In Edeirnion were-left those men, and because-of that was-put Seven Horsemen on the town.
sentences.i: Those men were left in Edeirnion, and that is why the township was named Saith Marchog.
sentences.n: yd edewit 'were left', impersonal preterite of adaw. o achaws hynny 'because of that'. y dodet … ar 'was put on' = was named, as with Gwern above. Seith Marchawc 'Seven Horsemen', modern Saith Marchog, in Edeirnion. y dref ← tref 'township', softened after the article (feminine).

sentences.t: Sef seithwyr oedynt, Cradawc uab Bran, ac Euehyd Hir, ac Unic Glew Yscwyd, ac Idic uab Anarawc Walltgrwn, a Fodor uab Eruyll, ac Wlch Minasgwrn, a Llashar uab Llayssar Llaesgygwyt, a Phendaran Dyuet dyuet yn was ieuanc gyt ac wy.
sentences.l: That-is the seven-men they-were: Caradog son of-Brân, and Efeydd Hir, and Unig Glew Ysgwydd, and Iddig son of-Anarawg Walltgrwn, and Ffodor son of-Erfyll, and Wlch Minasgwrn, and Llashar son of-Llasar Llaesgygwyd, and Pendaran Dyfed [Dyfed] as a-young lad with them.
sentences.i: The seven were Caradog son of Brân, Efeydd Hir, Unig Glew Ysgwydd, Iddig son of Anarawg Walltgrwn, Ffodor son of Erfyll, Wlch Minasgwrn, Llashar son of Llasar Llaesgygwyd, and with them Pendaran Dyfed, a young lad.
sentences.n: Sef seithwyr oedynt 'that is, the seven men they were'. Euehyd Hir is the Eueyd Hir of the last part, Efeydd Hir 'the Tall'; Unig Glew Ysgwydd and Iddig son of Anarawg were there too. Walltgrwn 'round-haired' (gwallt + crwn), one word as the witness prints it (Evans breaks the line after wallt). a Fodor: Ffodor, with F written for ff (/f/), as in a fawb below; ff does not change after a (the Red Book a ffodor). Minasgwrn and Llaesgygwyt are epithets of uncertain meaning; Llayssar is presumably the Llasar of the cauldron. a Phendaran ← Pendaran. Dyuet dyuet: Evans repeats dyuet across a line break, a dittography (the Red Book has a phendaram dyuet); kept as written, read once. yn was ieuanc 'as a young lad': gwas softened after yn. Pendaran makes an eighth, a page with the seven.

sentences.t: Y seith hynny a drigwys yn seith kynueissat y synyaw ar yr ynys honn, a Chradawc uab Bran yn benhaf kynweisyat arnunt.
sentences.l: Those seven it-was-that stayed as seven stewards to watch over this island, and Caradog son of-Brân as chiefest steward over-them.
sentences.i: Those seven stayed behind as seven stewards to keep watch over this island, with Caradog son of Brân as chief steward over them.
sentences.n: a drigwys ← trigwys, -wys preterite of trigyaw 'stay', softened after a, and singular after the plural subject placed first. kynueissat and kynweisyat are the same word spelt two ways, 'chief officer, steward' (cynweisiad). y synyaw ar 'to watch over'. yn benhaf ← pennaf, softened after yn. arnunt 'over them'.

sentences.t: Bendigeiduran, a'r yniuer a dywedyssam ni, a hwylyssant parth ac Iwerdon, ac nyt oed uawr y weilgi yna: y ueis yd aeth ef.
sentences.l: Bendigeidfran, and the company that we-spoke-of, it-was-that sailed towards Ireland, and was-not great the sea then: wading he-went.
sentences.i: Bendigeidfran and the host we have spoken of sailed for Ireland; and the sea was not wide then: he went across by wading.
sentences.n: a dywedyssam ni 'that we told of': the narrator's 'we', 1 pl. preterite. a hwylyssant 'sailed': here the verb after the subject placed first is plural (he and the host), though such a verb is often singular, as a drigwys in the last unit. y weilgi ← gweilgi 'open sea', softened after the article; uawr ← mawr after oed. y ueis 'to wading': beis 'shallow water, ford', softened after y 'to'; mynet y ueis is 'to go wading'.

sentences.t: Nyt oed namyn dwy auon: Lli ac Archan y gelwit.
sentences.l: There-was-not but two rivers: Lli and Archan they-were-called.
sentences.i: There were only two rivers, called Lli and Archan.
sentences.n: Nyt oed namyn 'there was not but' = there was only. dwy auon 'two rivers': dwy is the feminine 'two'. y gelwit 'they were called': gelwit, impersonal imperfect of galw (a > e). Lli and Archan are known only from this passage; what or where they were is uncertain (lli is also a common word for 'flood, current').

sentences.t: A guedy hynny yd amlawys y weilgi, pan oreskynwys y weilgi y tyrnassoed.
sentences.l: And after that grew the sea, when overran the sea the kingdoms.
sentences.i: And after that the sea grew wide, when it overran the kingdoms.
sentences.n: yd amlawys 'grew, multiplied', -wys preterite of amlhau (aml 'plentiful'). pan oreskynwys 'when it overran': goreskynwys, preterite of goresgyn 'conquer, overrun', softened after pan. y tyrnassoed 'the kingdoms' (teyrnasoedd).

sentences.t: Ac yna y kerdwys ef ac a oed o gerd arwest ar y geuyn e hun, a chyrchu tir Iwerdon.
sentences.l: And then he-walked he, and what was of music of-string on his back himself, and making-for the land of Ireland.
sentences.i: And then he walked over, with all the string-music there was on his own back, and made for the land of Ireland.
sentences.n: kerdwys 'walked', -wys preterite of kerdet. ac a oed 'and (with) all that there was'. o gerd ← kerd 'music, song', softened after o: these two words are written above the line in the manuscript (raised in Evans), and are taken into the line here. arwest 'string (of an instrument)': kerd arwest is string-music, standing for the harpers and their harps; the exact sense of arwest is uncertain. ar y geuyn e hun 'on his own back' (keuyn softened after y 'his'). a chyrchu ← kyrchu, spirant after a.

sentences.t: A meicheit Matholwch a oedynt ar lan y weilgi dydgueith, yn troi yg kylch eu moch.
sentences.l: And the swineherds of-Matholwch it-was-that were on the shore of the sea one-day, turning around their swine.
sentences.i: And Matholwch's swineherds were on the shore of the sea one day, tending their swine.
sentences.n: meicheit 'swineherds', plural of meichat (moch 'pigs'). a oedynt: the abnormal sentence, here with a plural verb. ar lan ← glan 'shore', softened after ar. yg kylch 'around' (yn + kylch, ynghylch); to turn about one's pigs is to tend them.

sentences.t: Ac o achaws dremynt a welsant ar y weilgi, wy a doethant at Matholwch.
sentences.l: And because-of a-sight that they-saw on the sea, they it-was-that came to Matholwch.
sentences.i: And because of a sight they saw on the sea, they came to Matholwch.
sentences.n: o achaws 'because of'. dremynt is tremynt 'sight, spectacle' in its softened form; Evans prints no e (= y 'the') before it, and the image agrees, though the second witness reads e dremynt 'the sight', which would explain the mutation. Read as written: 'a sight'. wy a doethant 'they came'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb vy, “henpych guell.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said they, “may-you-be better.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” they said, “hail to you.”
sentences.n: heb vy 'said they': vy is wy 'they' spelt with v, a one-off (the second witness agrees; elsewhere the scribe writes wy). henpych guell 'may you be better': henpych is the 2 sg. present subjunctive of hanbot (hanfod), a compound of bot, surviving in this greeting; guell 'better' (gwell): 'may you be better', a greeting, 'hail'.

sentences.t: “Duw a rodo da ywch,” heb ef, “a chwedleu genhwch.”
sentences.l: “God may-he-give good to-you,” said he, “and news with-you.”
sentences.i: “God give you good,” he said, “and what news have you?”
sentences.n: Duw a rodo da ywch: the formula of the last part, rodo the present subjunctive of wishing. chwedleu 'news', plural of chwedyl 'tale'; genhwch 'with you' (gan conjugated, 2 pl.): 'and news with you' asks for it.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb wy, “mae genhym ni chwedleu ryued: coet rywelsom ar y weilgi, yn y lle ny welsam eiryoet un prenn.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said they, “there-is with-us news strange: a-wood we-have-seen on the sea, in the place we-did-not-see ever one tree.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” they said, “we have strange news: we have seen a forest on the sea, where we never saw a single tree before.”
sentences.n: mae genhym ni 'is with us' = we have. ryued 'strange'. coet rywelsom 'a wood we have seen': the object first; ry- before the preterite makes it a perfect, 'have seen'. ny welsam 'we did not see'; eiryoet 'ever'. prenn 'tree'.

sentences.t: “Llyna beth eres,” heb ef. “A welewch wchi dim namyn hynny?”
sentences.l: “There-is a-thing strange,” said he. “Did-you-see you anything but that?”
sentences.i: “That is a strange thing,” he said. “Did you see anything besides?”
sentences.n: Llyna 'there is' (as llyma 'here is'); beth ← peth, softened after it. eres 'strange, marvellous'. A welewch 'did you see?': A is the question particle; welewch is the imperfect, 2 pl. wchi 'you', a spelling of chwi, the pronoun repeated after the verb. dim 'anything'.

sentences.t: “Gwelem, Arglwyd,” heb wy, “mynyd mawr gyr llaw y coet, a hwnnw ar gerdet; ac eskeir aruchel ar y mynyd, a llynn o pop parth y'r eskeir; a'r coet, a'r mynyd, a phob peth oll o hynny ar gerdet.”
sentences.l: “We-saw, Lord,” said they, “a-mountain great beside the wood, and that-one on the move; and a-ridge very-high on the mountain, and a-lake on each side of the ridge; and the wood, and the mountain, and every thing all of that on the move.”
sentences.i: “We did, Lord,” they said: “a great mountain beside the forest, and the mountain moving; and a towering ridge on the mountain, and a lake on either side of the ridge; and the forest and the mountain and all of it moving.”
sentences.n: Gwelem 'we saw': the answer repeats the verb, here 1 pl. imperfect. gyr llaw 'beside' (ger llaw). ar gerdet 'on the go, moving': kerdet softened after ar. eskeir 'ridge' (esgair, literally 'shank'). aruchel 'very high' (ar- + uchel). o pop parth 'on each side': pop is pob with -p for -b, left unsoftened after o here (in the next answer the same phrase is written o bop).

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu, “nyt oes neb yma a wypo dim y wrth hynny, onys gwyr Branwen. Gouynnwch idi.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part, “there-is-not anyone here who may-know anything about that, unless-it knows Branwen. Ask to-her.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said, “there is no one here who would know anything of that, unless Branwen knows. Ask her.”
sentences.n: a wypo 'who may know': present subjunctive of gwybot, after a negative. y wrth 'about'. onys gwyr 'unless she knows it': ony 'if not' + infixed -s 'it'; gwyr is 'knows', 3 sg. present of gwybot, not gwyr 'men'. Gouynnwch idi 'ask her': the person asked takes y 'to'.

sentences.t: Kennadeu a aeth at Uranwen.
sentences.l: Messengers it-was-that went to Branwen.
sentences.i: Messengers went to Branwen.
sentences.n: a aeth is singular after the plural kennadeu placed first, as A chenadeu a aeth in the last part. at Uranwen ← Branwen, softened after at.

sentences.t: “Arglwydes,” heb wy, “beth dybygy di yw hynny?”
sentences.l: “Lady,” said they, “what do-you-suppose you is that?”
sentences.i: “Lady,” they said, “what do you think that is?”
sentences.n: Arglwydes 'lady', the feminine of arglwyd. beth ← peth 'what'. dybygy ← tybygy, 2 sg. present of tybygu 'suppose', softened after beth (the relative a understood).

sentences.t: “Kyn ny bwyf arglwydes,” heb hi, “mi a wnn beth yw hynny: gwyr Ynys y Kedyrn yn dyuot drwod o glybot uym poen a'm amharch.”
sentences.l: “Though I-may-not-be lady,” said she, “I it-is-that know what is that: the men of-the-Island of-the-Mighty coming across from hearing my pain and my dishonour.”
sentences.i: “Though I am no lady,” she said, “I know what that is: the men of the Island of the Mighty coming over, having heard of my suffering and my dishonour.”
sentences.n: Kyn ny bwyf 'though I may not be': kyn 'though', bwyf the present subjunctive of bot — a bitter answer from a woman set to bake. mi a wnn 'I know': gwnn softened after a (Evans's a wnn, checked on the image). drwod 'across, over'. uym poen 'my pain' (uym = fy); a'm amharch 'and my dishonour'.

sentences.t: “Beth yw y coet a welat ar y mor?” heb wy.
sentences.l: “What is the wood that was-seen on the sea?” said they.
sentences.i: “What is the forest that was seen on the sea?” they said.
sentences.n: a welat 'that was seen': an impersonal preterite in -at (as cahat 'was got'), beside a welit in the next question. y mor 'the sea', the everyday word beside gweilgi.

sentences.t: “Gwernenni llongeu a hwylbrenni,” heb hi.
sentences.l: “Masts of-ships and sail-poles,” said she.
sentences.i: “The masts and spars of ships,” she said.
sentences.n: gwernenni, plural of gwernen 'alder', used of masts (alder poles) — and alder is gwern, her son's name. hwylbrenni 'sail-poles' (hwyl 'sail' + prenn 'tree, wood', softened in the compound).

sentences.t: “Och,” heb wy, “beth oed y mynyd a welit gan ystlys y llongeu?”
sentences.l: “Och,” said they, “what was the mountain that was-seen by the side of the ships?”
sentences.i: “Oh,” they said, “what was the mountain that was seen beside the ships?”
sentences.n: Och, a cry of dismay (rendered as in the earlier parts). a welit 'that was seen': impersonal imperfect (-it), beside welat above. gan ystlys 'by the side of' (ystlys 'side, flank').

sentences.t: “Bendigeiduran uym brawt,” heb hi, “oed hwnnw, yn dyuot y ueis. Nyt oed long y kynghanei ef yndi.”
sentences.l: “Bendigeidfran my brother,” said she, “was that-one, coming wading. There-was-not a-ship that he-would-fit in-it.”
sentences.i: “That was Bendigeidfran my brother,” she said, “coming over by wading. There was no ship he would fit in.”
sentences.n: Bendigeiduran … oed hwnnw: the predicate first, 'Bendigeidfran … was that one'. y ueis 'wading', as above. Nyt oed long: Evans prints Nyt (the second witness Nyd); long ← llong, softened after oed. y kynghanei 'that he would fit': imperfect of genni (MW also gannu) 'be contained, have room', here compounded with kyn- (the g written gh, as in kynghor); the simplex follows below in enghis, ganho, ganhei, and compare ny angassei 'had not fitted' in the last part. The Red Book has the same compound (kyghanei). yndi 'in it' (feminine, for llong).

sentences.t: “Beth oed yr eskeir aruchel a'r llynn o bop parth y'r eskeir?”
sentences.l: “What was the ridge very-high and the lake on each side of the ridge?”
sentences.i: “What was the towering ridge, and the lake on either side of the ridge?”
sentences.n: No heb tag: the messengers are understood. o bop parth: pob softened after o, its final b written p.

sentences.t: “Ef,” heb hi, “yn edrych ar yr ynys honn, llidyawc yw. Y deu lygat ef o pop parth y drwyn yw y dwy lynn o bop parth y'r eskeir.”
sentences.l: “He,” said she, “looking at this island, angry he-is. The two eyes of-him on each side of his nose are the two lakes on each side of the ridge.”
sentences.i: “That is he,” she said, “looking at this island; he is angry. His two eyes on either side of his nose are the two lakes on either side of the ridge.”
sentences.n: Ef … llidyawc yw 'he … angry he is': the subject set out first, then the sentence. y deu lygat ef 'his two eyes': y … ef 'his'; lygat ← llygat, softened after deu. o pop parth is again unsoftened after o (the Red Book too), beside o bop at the end of the sentence. y drwyn ← trwyn 'his nose'. y dwy lynn 'the two lakes': llynn is usually masculine, but here it is counted with the feminine dwy and softened after it (the Red Book has the same).

sentences.t: Ac yna dygyuor holl wyr ymlad Iwerdon a wnaethpwyt y gyt, a'r holl uorbennyd yn gyflym, a chynghor a gymerwyt.
sentences.l: And then mustering all the men of-fighting of-Ireland was-done together, and all the great-chiefs quickly, and counsel was-taken.
sentences.i: And then all the fighting men of Ireland were mustered, and all the great lords, in haste, and counsel was taken.
sentences.n: dygyuor … a wnaethpwyt 'mustering was done', the gwneuthur pattern with the impersonal. holl 'all' stands before its noun and softens it: holl wyr ← gwyr. uorbennyd ← morbennyd, apparently 'great chiefs' (mawr 'great' + penn 'head'; mor 'sea' + penn has also been thought of); a rare word and uncertain, softened after holl. a gymerwyt ← kymerwyt, impersonal preterite of kymryt.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb y wyrda wrth Uatholwch, “nyt oes gynghor namyn kilyaw drwy Linon (auon oed yn Iwerdon), a gadu Llinon y rot ac ef, a thorri y bont yssyd ar yr auon.
sentences.l: “Lord,” said his noblemen to Matholwch, “there-is-not counsel but retreating across Llinon (a-river that-was in Ireland), and leaving Llinon between-you and him, and breaking the bridge that-is on the river.
sentences.i: “Lord,” said his noblemen to Matholwch, “there is no counsel but to fall back across the Llinon (a river there was in Ireland), and leave the Llinon between you and him, and break the bridge that is over the river.
sentences.n: y wyrda ← gwyrda 'his noblemen'. gynghor ← kynghor, softened after nyt oes (like lonyd above). kilyaw 'retreat'. drwy Linon ← Llinon, softened after drwy; the narrator's aside is put in brackets. y rot ac ef 'between you and him': y rot is the regular 2 sg. of the conjugated preposition y rwng 'between' (modern rhyngot), as y rof i a Duw 'between me and God' is the 1 sg.; it occurred in the First Branch (y rot a'th uarchogyon), and the Red Book has the same here. Compare y rydunt 'between them' at the end of this part. a thorri ← torri, spirant after a. y bont ← pont, softened after the article (feminine). yssyd 'that is'.

sentences.t: A mein sugyn yssyd y gwaelawt yr auon, ny eill na llong na llestyr arnei.”
sentences.l: And sucking stones there-are in-the bottom of the river, (and) cannot either ship or vessel (be) on-it.”
sentences.i: And there are sucking stones in the bed of the river, so that neither ship nor vessel can go upon it.”
sentences.n: mein 'stones' (maen). mein sugyn 'stones of suction' (sugn 'sucking'): perhaps lodestones, perhaps a bed that sucks things down; the phrase is uncertain. y gwaelawt 'in the bottom': yn + gwaelawt with the nasal mutation, written y gwaelawt as with y mywn; Evans prints ygwaelawt as one word, and the division is ours. ny eill 'cannot' (gall, softened, the g lost). na … na 'neither … nor'. llestyr 'vessel'. arnei 'on it' (the river, feminine).

sentences.t: Wynt a gylyssant drwy yr auon, ac a torryssant y bont.
sentences.l: They it-was-that retreated across the river, and broke the bridge.
sentences.i: They fell back across the river and broke down the bridge.
sentences.n: a gylyssant ← kilyssant, 3 pl. preterite of kilyaw (i written y), softened after a. a torryssant is left unsoftened after a, where a dorryssant would be expected; the Red Book too has ac a torrassant (and y pont, also unsoftened).

sentences.t: Bendigeiduran a doeth y'r tir, a llynghes y gyt ac ef, parth a glann yr auon.
sentences.l: Bendigeidfran it-was-that came to the land, and a-fleet together with him, towards the bank of the river.
sentences.i: Bendigeidfran came ashore, and a fleet with him, towards the bank of the river.
sentences.n: a doeth 'came'. llynghes 'fleet' (llynges): Evans prints llynghes, the second witness llynges. glann 'bank'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb y wyrda, “ti a wdost kennedyf yr auon, ny eill neb uynet drwydi, nyt oes bont arnei hitheu. Mae dy gynghor am bont?” heb wy.
sentences.l: “Lord,” said his noblemen, “you it-is-that know the property of the river: no-one can go through-it, there-is-not a-bridge on-it for-its-part. Where-is your counsel about a-bridge?” said they.
sentences.i: “Lord,” said his noblemen, “you know the nature of the river: no one can cross it, and there is no bridge over it. What is your counsel about a bridge?” they said.
sentences.n: These are Bendigeidfran's own noblemen. a wdost 'know': gwdost, 2 sg. present of gwybot, softened after a. kennedyf 'property, peculiar nature' — Evans's spelling (the witness kynnedyf), modern cynneddf; compare chynnedyf y peir 'the property of the cauldron' in the last part. drwydi 'through it' (trwy conjugated, feminine). bont ← pont after oes. hitheu 'it for its part': Evans has the h written above hiteu, taken into the line here. Mae 'where is?', used to ask 'what is'.

sentences.t: “Nit oes,” heb ynteu, “namyn a uo penn bit pont. Mi a uydaf pont,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “There-is-not,” said he-for-his-part, “but whoever-may-be head let-him-be bridge. I it-is-that will-be bridge,” said he.
sentences.i: “There is none,” he said, “but this: he who would be a chief, let him be a bridge. I will be the bridge,” he said.
sentences.n: Nit oes 'there is not', answering the question. a uo penn bit pont 'who may be head, let him be bridge': uo, present subjunctive of bot, softened after a; bit, the old 3 sg. imperative of bot, 'let him be'. The saying is proverbial, as the next sentence says. Mi a uydaf 'I will be': bydaf, future of bot, softened after a.

sentences.t: Ac yna gyntaf y dywetpwyt y geir hwnnw, ac y diharebir etwa ohonaw.
sentences.l: And then first was-said that saying, and it-is-proverbed still from-it.
sentences.i: And it was then that the saying was first spoken, and it is still used as a proverb.
sentences.n: gyntaf ← kyntaf 'first', softened as an adverb. dywetpwyt, impersonal preterite of dywedut. y geir hwnnw 'that word, saying'. diharebir 'is proverbed', present impersonal (-ir) of diharebu, from dihareb 'proverb'. etwa 'still'. ohonaw 'of it' (o conjugated).

sentences.t: Ac yna guedy gorwed ohonaw ef ar traws yr auon, y byrwyt clwydeu arnaw ef, ac yd aeth y luoed ef ar y draws ef drwod.
sentences.l: And then after lying of-him he across the river, were-thrown hurdles on-him he, and went his hosts he across-him over.
sentences.i: And then, when he had lain down across the river, hurdles were laid on him, and his hosts went over across him.
sentences.n: guedy gorwed ohonaw ef 'after his lying down': the subject of a verbal noun is given with o 'of', here conjugated, ohonaw. ar traws 'across' (unsoftened here; ar y draws ef 'across him' has traws softened after y 'his'). y byrwyt 'were thrown': impersonal preterite of bwrw. clwydeu 'hurdles', wattle frames. y luoed ← lluoed 'his hosts'. drwod 'over'.

sentences.t: Ar hynny, gyt ac y kyuodes ef, llyma gennadeu Matholwch yn dyuot attaw ef, ac yn kyuarch guell idaw, ac yn y annerch y gan Uatholwch y gyuathrachwr, ac yn menegi o'e uod ef na haedei arnaw ef namyn da.
sentences.l: At that, as-soon-as he-rose he, behold messengers of-Matholwch coming to-him he, and greeting to-him, and his saluting from Matholwch his kinsman-by-marriage, and telling, of his will he, that he-deserved not from-him he but good.
sentences.i: Thereupon, as soon as he rose, there were Matholwch's messengers coming to him, greeting him and saluting him from Matholwch his kinsman by marriage, and telling him that, as far as Matholwch's will went, he had earned nothing at his hands but good.
sentences.n: gyt ac 'as soon as'. kyuodes 'rose', 3 sg. preterite in -es of kyuodi. llyma gennadeu ← kennadeu, softened after llyma. kyuarch guell 'greeting', as in the last part. y annerch 'his saluting'; y gan 'from, on behalf of'. y gyuathrachwr ← kyuathrachwr 'kinsman by marriage' (compare ymgyuathrachu in the last part). o'e uod ef 'of his will': bod 'will', softened after 'e. haedei 'deserved', imperfect of haedu; arnaw 'at his hands'.

sentences.t: “Ac y mae Matholwch yn rodi brenhinaeth Iwerdon y Wern uab Matholwch, dy nei ditheu, uab dy chwaer, ac yn y ystynnu y'th wyd di, yn lle y cam a'r codyant a wnaethpwyt y Uranwen.
sentences.l: “And Matholwch is giving the kingship of Ireland to Gwern son of-Matholwch, your nephew you-for-your-part, son of your sister, and its conferring in your-presence you, in place of the wrong and the hurt that was-done to Branwen.
sentences.i: “And Matholwch is giving the kingship of Ireland to Gwern son of Matholwch, your own nephew, your sister's son, and conferring it on him in your presence, in amends for the wrong and the hurt that were done to Branwen.
sentences.n: y mae 'is', the form used after the particle y. brenhinaeth 'kingship'. y Wern ← Gwern, softened after y 'to'. dy nei ditheu 'your nephew': ditheu ← titheu 'you for your part'. y ystynnu 'its extending, conferring'. y'th wyd di 'in your presence': y (= yn) + 'th 'your' + gwyd 'presence', softened after 'th. yn lle 'in place of'. codyant 'affliction, hurt'. y Uranwen ← Branwen.

sentences.t: Ac yn y lle y mynnych ditheu, ay yma ay yn Ynys y Kedyrn, gossymdeitha Uatholwch.”
sentences.l: And in the place you-may-wish you-for-your-part, either here or in the Island of the Mighty, maintain Matholwch.”
sentences.i: And wherever you wish, either here or in the Island of the Mighty, provide for Matholwch.”
sentences.n: y mynnych 'that you may wish', present subjunctive of mynnu. ay … ay 'either … or'. gossymdeitha is the imperative of gossymdeithaw 'maintain, provide a living for' (the last part had yu gossymdeithaw 'to keep them'): Matholwch offers to live as Bendigeidfran's dependent wherever he likes; the exact force here is uncertain. Uatholwch ← Matholwch, softened as the object.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb ynteu Uendigeiduran, “ony allaf i ue hun cael y urenhinaeth, ac aduyd ys kymeraf gynghor am ych kennadwri chwi. O hyn hyt ban del amgen, ny cheffwch y genhyf i attep.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said he-for-his-part Bendigeidfran, “unless I-can I myself get the kingship, and perhaps I-will-take counsel about your message you. From this until when may-come other, you-will-not-get from-me I an-answer.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said Bendigeidfran, “unless I may have the kingship myself, perhaps I will take counsel on your message. From now until something else comes, you will get no answer from me.”
sentences.n: ony allaf i 'unless I can': gallaf softened after ony. ue hun 'myself'. y urenhinaeth ← brenhinaeth, softened after the article (feminine). ac aduyd 'and perhaps': the Red Book writes atuyd, the word for 'perhaps'; its make-up is not certain; ys before kymeraf is perhaps the particle or the infixed 'it'. kennadwri 'message'. ban del amgen 'when something else may come': ban = pan, del present subjunctive of dyuot, amgen 'other'. ny cheffwch 'you will not get': keffwch, present of kaffael, spirant after ny.

sentences.t: “Ie,” heb wynteu, “yr atteb goreu a gaffom ninheu, attat ti y down ac ef, ac aro ditheu yn kennadwri ninheu.”
sentences.l: “Yes,” said they-for-their-part, “the answer best that we-may-get we-for-our-part, to you we-will-come with it, and wait you-for-your-part for our message we-for-our-part.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” they said, “the best answer we can get, we will bring it to you; and wait you for our message.”
sentences.n: a gaffom 'that we may get': present subjunctive of kaffael, softened after a. attat ti 'to you' (Evans attat, the witness atat). y down 'we will come': down, 1 pl. present of dyuot, used of the future. ac ef 'with it'. aro 'wait', imperative of aros; yn kennadwri 'in (expectation of) the message'.

sentences.t: “Arhoaf,” heb ef, “o dowch yn ehegyr.”
sentences.l: “I-will-wait,” said he, “if you-come quickly.”
sentences.i: “I will wait,” he said, “if you come quickly.”
sentences.n: Arhoaf 'I will wait': the answer repeats the verb. o dowch 'if you come': o 'if', dowch 2 pl. present of dyuot. ehegyr: probably 'swiftly, readily'; the word is rare and its meaning uncertain (the Red Book has instead yn ebrwyd 'quickly').

sentences.t: Y kennadeu a gyrchyssant racdu, ac at Uatholwch y doethant.
sentences.l: The messengers it-was-that went onward, and to Matholwch they-came.
sentences.i: The messengers went on their way and came to Matholwch.
sentences.n: a gyrchyssant ← kyrchyssant 'made for', 3 pl. preterite, softened after a. racdu 'onward' (rac 'before', conjugated). at Uatholwch y doethant 'to Matholwch they came': the phrase first, so the verb takes y.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb wy, “kyweira attep a uo gwell at Uendigeidwran. Ny warandawei dim o'r attep a aeth y genhym ni attaw ef.”
sentences.l: “Lord,” said they, “prepare an-answer that may-be better to Bendigeidfran. He-would-not-listen-to anything of the answer that went from-us we to-him.”
sentences.i: “Lord,” they said, “make ready a better answer for Bendigeidfran. He would not listen to any of the answer we took him.”
sentences.n: kyweira 'make ready', imperative of kyweiraw. a uo gwell 'that may be better'. Uendigeidwran: here the softened b of bran is written w (-dwran), where the rest of the part writes Uendigeiduran; the same name. Ny warandawei 'he would not listen to': imperfect of gwarandaw, softened after ny. y genhym ni 'from us' (y gan, conjugated).

sentences.t: “A wyr,” heb y Matholwch, “mae ych kynghor chwi?”
sentences.l: “O men,” said Matholwch, “where-is your counsel you?”
sentences.i: “Men,” said Matholwch, “what is your counsel?”
sentences.n: A wyr 'O men': the vocative particle a softens gwyr, as in the last part. heb y Matholwch: y before the name, as in heb y brenhin. mae 'where is?', asking 'what is'.

sentences.t: “Arglwyd,” heb wy, “nyt oes it gynghor namyn un. Ni enghis ef y mywn ty eiryoet,” heb wy.
sentences.l: “Lord,” said they, “there-is-not to-you counsel but one. He-has-not-fitted he inside a-house ever,” said they.
sentences.i: “Lord,” they said, “you have but one course. No house has ever been able to hold him,” they said.
sentences.n: it 'to you' (y conjugated, 2 sg.). In the manuscript there are blank spaces here, after heb wy and after gynghor, where the vellum is flawed; nothing is lost to the sense, and the text is printed continuously. enghis 'fitted, was held': genghis, 3 sg. preterite (-is) of genni 'be contained, have room' (stem gang-, a > e before -is), softened after Ni, the g dropping away, as ny angassei in the last part (the Red Book here nyt eigwys). y mywn 'inside': our word division.

sentences.t: “Gwna ty,” heb wy, “o'y anryded ef, y ganho ef a gwyr Ynys y Kedyrn yn y neill parth y'r ty, a thitheu a'th lu yn y parth arall. A doro dy urenhinaeth yn y ewyllus, a gwra idaw.
sentences.l: “Make a-house,” said they, “for his rank he, that may-fit he and the men of-the-Island of-the-Mighty in the one side of the house, and you-for-your-part and your host in the other side. And give your kingship into his will, and do-homage to-him.
sentences.i: “Build a house,” they said, “befitting his rank, to hold him and the men of the Island of the Mighty in one half of it, and you and your host in the other. And put your kingship at his will, and do him homage.
sentences.n: Gwna 'make', imperative of gwneuthur. o'y anryded ef 'for his rank'. y ganho ef a gwyr … 'that he and the men … may fit': ef and gwyr are the subject, not the object; present subjunctive of genni 'be contained, have room', the simplex of kynghanei above; ganho is the radical form, since the particle y does not mutate (the Red Book has y geingho). a thitheu ← titheu, spirant after a; a'th lu ← llu 'your host', softened after 'th. A doro 'and give': doro, imperative of rodi. yn y ewyllus 'into his will'. gwra idaw 'do homage to him': imperative of gwrhau 'become (someone's) man'.

sentences.t: Ac o enryded gwneuthur y ty,” heb wy, “peth ny chauas eiryoet ty y ganhei yndaw, ef a tangnoueda a thi.”
sentences.l: And from the rank of making the house,” said they, “a-thing he-never-got ever, a-house that-he-could-fit in-it, he it-is-that will-make-peace with you.”
sentences.i: And for the rank shown him in building the house — a thing he has never had, a house he could fit in — he will make peace with you.”
sentences.n: enryded is anryded with e. ny chauas 'he did not get': cauas, preterite of kaffael, spirant after ny. y ganhei yndaw 'that he could fit in': ganhei, imperfect of the same verb as ganho; yndaw 'in it' (masculine, for ty). ef a tangnoueda 'he will make peace': tangnouedu (from tangneued 'peace'), left unsoftened after a, where a dangnoueda would be expected (the Red Book too has a tangneuedha). a thi ← ti, spirant after a 'with'.

sentences.t: A'r kennadeu a doethant a'r gennadwri honno gantunt at Uendigeiduran; ac ynteu a gymerth gynghor.
sentences.l: And the messengers it-was-that came with that message with-them to Bendigeidfran; and he-for-his-part took counsel.
sentences.i: And the messengers brought that message to Bendigeidfran, and he took counsel.
sentences.n: a'r gennadwri ← kennadwri 'message', softened after the article (feminine). gantunt 'with them'. a gymerth ← kymerth, preterite of kymryt, softened after a.

sentences.t: Sef a gauas yn y gynghor, kymryt hynny; a thrwy gynghor Branuen uu hynny oll, ac rac llygru y wlat oed genti hitheu hynny.
sentences.l: That-is what he-got in his counsel: taking that; and through the counsel of Branwen was that all, and for-fear-of spoiling the land was with-her she-for-her-part that.
sentences.i: What he resolved in council was to accept it; and all that was by Branwen's counsel, and it was for fear of the land being laid waste that she was for it.
sentences.n: Sef a gauas yn y gynghor 'that is what he got in his council', as Sef a gahat yn y kynghor in the last part. uu ← bu, the verb before its subject hynny oll. rac llygru y wlat 'for fear of spoiling the country': rac 'against, lest'; y wlat ← gwlat, softened after the article. oed genti hitheu hynny 'that was with her' = that was her mind.

sentences.t: E tangneued a gyweirwyt, a'r ty a adeilwyt yn uawr ac yn braf.
sentences.l: The peace was-made-ready, and the house was-built great and stout.
sentences.i: The peace was made ready, and the house was built, great and stout.
sentences.n: E is y 'the'. a gyweirwyt ← kyweirwyt, impersonal preterite of kyweiraw 'arrange, make ready', softened after a. a adeilwyt 'was built'. yn uawr 'great' (mawr). yn braf is most likely praff 'thick, stout, massive', softened after yn (p > b) like yn uawr, with f written for ff (as in a fawb below); the Red Book writes yn braff. It is not modern braf 'fine'.

sentences.t: Ac ystryw a wnaeth y Gwydyl.
sentences.l: And a-trick it-was-that the Irish did.
sentences.i: And the Irish played a trick.
sentences.n: ystryw 'stratagem, trick', the object first. a wnaeth is singular, as usual before a noun subject. y Gwydyl 'the Irish', plural of Gwydel 'Irishman'.

sentences.t: Sef ystryw a wnaethant, dodi guanas o bop parth y bop colouyn o cant colouyn oed yn y ty, a dodi boly croyn ar bop guanas, a gwr aruawc ym pob vn ohonunt.
sentences.l: That-is the trick they-did: putting a-peg on every side of every pillar of the hundred pillars that-were in the house, and putting a-bag of-hide on every peg, and an-armed man in every one of-them.
sentences.i: The trick they played was to set a peg on either side of each of the hundred pillars in the house, and hang a hide bag on every peg, with an armed man in each.
sentences.n: Sef ystryw a wnaethant 'that is the trick they did', then the verbal nouns. guanas 'peg, hook' (gwanas). y bop colouyn 'to each pillar': pob softened after y. o cant colouyn 'of a hundred pillars': cant left unsoftened after o (so also the Red Book). boly croyn 'a hide bag': boly 'bag, belly', croyn 'hide' (croen). aruawc 'armed'. ym pob ← yn pob, n > m before p. vn is un (v for u). ohonunt 'of them'.

sentences.t: Sef a wnaeth Efnyssyen, dyuot ymlaen llu Ynys y Kedyrn y mywn, ac edrych golygon orwyllt antrugarawc ar hyt y ty.
sentences.l: That-is what Efnysien did: coming in-front-of the host of-the-Island of-the-Mighty inside, and looking looks frenzied merciless along the house.
sentences.i: What Efnysien did was to come in ahead of the host of the Island of the Mighty and cast fierce, merciless looks about the house.
sentences.n: Sef a wnaeth 'that is what … did', followed by verbal nouns. Efnyssyen is Efnysien (Efnyssen in the last part). ymlaen 'in front of' (yn + blaen). y mywn 'inside'. golygon 'looks, glances'. orwyllt ← gorwyllt 'frenzied, very wild' (gor- + gwyllt), here softened. antrugarawc 'merciless' (an- + trugarawc). ar hyt 'along, all through'.

sentences.t: Ac arganuot y bolyeu crwyn a wnaeth ar hyt y pyst.
sentences.l: And noticing the bags of-hide he-did along the posts.
sentences.i: And he caught sight of the hide bags all along the posts.
sentences.n: arganuot … a wnaeth 'noticing he did'. bolyeu, plural of boly; crwyn, plural of croen. pyst 'posts', plural of post.

sentences.t: “Beth yssyd yn y boly hwnn?” heb ef, wrth un o'r Guydyl.
sentences.l: “What is in this bag?” said he, to one of the Irish.
sentences.i: “What is in this bag?” he said to one of the Irish.
sentences.n: yssyd 'that is', the relative form of bot. Guydyl: Evans prints Guydyl here (gu for gw), the witness Gwydyl.

sentences.t: “Blawt, eneit,” heb ef.
sentences.l: “Flour, soul,” said he.
sentences.i: “Flour, friend,” he said.
sentences.n: Blawt 'flour, meal'. eneit 'soul', a familiar form of address, 'friend, my dear'.

sentences.t: Sef a wnaeth ynteu, y deimlaw hyt ban gauas y benn, a guascu y benn, yny glyw y uyssed yn ymanodi yn y ureichell drwy yr ascwrn.
sentences.l: That-is what he-did he-for-his-part: his feeling until he-got his head, and squeezing his head, until he-feels his fingers ymanodi-ing in the brain through the bone.
sentences.i: So he felt the man until he found his head, and squeezed the head until he felt his fingers sink into the brain through the bone.
sentences.n: y deimlaw 'his feeling': teimlaw softened after y 'his' (the man in the bag). ban gauas 'until he got': cauas, preterite of kaffael, softened after ban. y benn ← penn 'his head'. guascu 'squeezing'. yny glyw 'until he feels': clyw, present of clywet 'hear, feel', softened after yny — a vivid present in past narrative. y uyssed ← bysed 'his fingers'. ymanodi is rare, apparently 'sink in' or 'meet together'; ureichell ← breichell is obscure too, taken from the context as 'brain' (the Red Book prints yny vreithell, i.e. ← breithell); both are uncertain.

sentences.t: Ac adaw hwnnw, a dodi y law ar un arall a gouyn, “Beth yssyd yma?”
sentences.l: And leaving that-one, and putting his hand on one other and asking, “What is here?”
sentences.i: And he left that one, and put his hand on another, and asked, “What is in here?”
sentences.n: Verbal nouns carry the narrative on. y law ← llaw 'his hand'. In the manuscript there is a short line before adodi and a space between un and arall, a flaw; nothing is lost, and the text is printed continuously.

sentences.t: “Blawt,” medei y Gwydel.
sentences.l: “Flour,” said the Irishman.
sentences.i: “Flour,” said the Irishman.
sentences.n: medei 'said': imperfect of the defective verb meddaf 'say' (it has no verbal noun), a change from heb. Gwydel 'Irishman'.

sentences.t: Sef a wnai ynteu yr un guare a fawb ohonunt, hyt nat edewis ef wr byw o'r hollwyr o'r deu cannwr eithyr un.
sentences.l: That-is what he-did he-for-his-part: the same game with everyone of-them, until he-did-not-leave a-man alive of the all-men of the two hundred-men except one.
sentences.i: He played the same game with every one of them, until he had left not a man alive of all the two hundred but one.
sentences.n: a wnai 'he did', imperfect of gwneuthur, of a thing done over and over. guare 'game, sport'. a fawb is a phawb 'with everyone': pawb with the spirant after a 'with', the ph written f, as in y foen above (the Red Book has a phawb). edewis 'left', preterite of adaw. wr ← gwr. o'r hollwyr 'of all the men' (holl + gwyr). deu cannwr 'two hundred men' (cant + gwr); two to each of the hundred pillars. eithyr 'except'.

sentences.t: A dyuot at hwnnw, a gouyn, “Beth yssyd yma?”
sentences.l: And coming to that-one, and asking, “What is here?”
sentences.i: And he came to that one and asked, “What is in here?”
sentences.n: Verbal nouns again for the finite verbs; hwnnw 'that one', the last man.

sentences.t: “Blawt, eneit,” heb y Gwydel.
sentences.l: “Flour, soul,” said the Irishman.
sentences.i: “Flour, friend,” said the Irishman.
sentences.n: heb y Gwydel 'said the Irishman': heb takes y before a noun subject. eneit as before.

sentences.t: Sef a wnaeth ynteu, y deimlaw ef yny gauas y benn, ac ual y guascassei benneu y rei ereill, guascu penn hwnnw.
sentences.l: That-is what he-did he-for-his-part: his feeling him until he-got his head, and as he-had-squeezed the heads of the others, squeezing the head of that-one.
sentences.i: He felt him until he found his head, and as he had squeezed the heads of the others, he squeezed that man's head.
sentences.n: y deimlaw ef 'his feeling', as above. guascassei 'had squeezed': the pluperfect in -assei. benneu ← penneu 'heads', softened as object. y rei ereill 'the others'.

sentences.t: Sef y clywei arueu am benn hwnnw.
sentences.l: That-is (what) he-felt: armour about the head of that-one.
sentences.i: He felt armour about that man's head.
sentences.n: Sef again introduces what was found. clywei, imperfect of clywet 'hear, feel'. arueu 'arms, armour'. am benn ← penn, softened after am.

sentences.t: Nyt ymedewis ef a hwnnw, yny ladawd.
sentences.l: He-did-not-leave-off he with that-one, until he-killed (him).
sentences.i: He did not let go of him until he had killed him.
sentences.n: ymedewis 'parted', preterite of ymadaw 'leave off' (ym- + adaw); ymadaw a 'leave off with'. yny ladawd 'until he killed (him)': lladawd, the -awd preterite of llad, softened after yny.

sentences.t: Ac yna canu englyn:
sentences.l: And then singing an-englyn:
sentences.i: And then he sang an englyn:
sentences.n: canu 'singing', a verbal noun for the verb. englyn: a short stanza in strict metre; the one that follows is of an old three-line kind, and its words are hard.

sentences.t: “Yssit yn y boly hwnn amryw ulawt, keimeit, kynniuyeit, diskynneit yn trin, rac kydwyr cad barawt.”
sentences.l: “There-is in this bag a-different flour: champions, warriors, descenders in battle, before fellow-men battle-ready.”
sentences.i: “There is in this bag a different kind of flour: champions, warriors, men who come down into battle, ready for war before their comrades.”
sentences.n: An old englyn, set here as prose; every rendering of it is tentative. Yssit 'there is', an old form of yssyd used as the main verb. amryw ulawt 'a different (or mixed) flour': ulawt ← blawt, softened after amryw. keimeit 'champions'. kynniuyeit seems a plural of kynniuyat 'warrior' (cynif 'battle, toil'); its sense is uncertain. diskynneit 'those who come down', attackers. yn trin 'in battle'. rac kydwyr: rac 'before' or 'against', kydwyr 'fellow-men, comrades' (kyd- + gwyr); whether the foe or the warriors' own fellows are meant is unclear. cad barawt 'battle-ready': cad 'battle' + parawt 'ready', softened after the feminine noun cad; two words in Evans, with a clear space on the image (the witness cadbarawt, the Red Book cat barawt, with kytwyr for kydwyr).

sentences.t: Ac ar hynny y dothyw y niueroed y'r ty.
sentences.l: And at that came the hosts to the house.
sentences.i: And thereupon the companies came into the house.
sentences.n: dothyw 'came': an old perfect of dyuot. y niueroed 'the hosts' (niuer, the same word as yniuer). y'r ty: Evans prints yr ty, which is y 'to' + 'r 'the', written y'r here.

sentences.t: Ac y doeth gwyr Ynys Iwerdon y'r ty o'r neill parth, a gwyr Ynys y Kedyrn o'r parth arall.
sentences.l: And came the men of-the-Island of-Ireland to the house from the one side, and the men of-the-Island of-the-Mighty from the other side.
sentences.i: The men of the Island of Ireland came into the house on one side, and the men of the Island of the Mighty on the other.
sentences.n: doeth is singular before the plural subject gwyr. Ynys Iwerdon 'the Island of Ireland', set against Ynys y Kedyrn. o'r neill parth … o'r parth arall 'from the one side … from the other side'.

sentences.t: Ac yn gyn ebrwydet ac yd eistedyssant y bu duundeb y rydunt, ac yd ystynnwyt y urenhinaeth y'r mab.
sentences.l: And as quickly as they-sat-down was agreement between-them, and was-conferred the kingship to the boy.
sentences.i: And as soon as they had sat down there was concord between them, and the kingship was conferred on the boy.
sentences.n: yn gyn ebrwydet ac 'as swiftly as': gyn ← kyn 'as', softened after yn, with ebrwydet, the equative of ebrwyd 'swift'. eistedyssant 'they sat'. duundeb 'agreement, concord'. y rydunt 'between them' (rwng conjugated). ystynnwyt 'was conferred', impersonal preterite of ystynnu, as in Matholwch's offer. y'r mab: Evans prints yr mab, written y'r here.

about: Matholwch takes Branwen home to Ireland, where she is honoured and bears him a son, Gwern; but in the second year the Irish stir up the insult he suffered in Wales, and she is turned out of his chamber, set to bake in the court and struck every day. She rears a starling and sends it with a letter to her brother Bendigeidfran, who leaves seven stewards to keep the Island of the Mighty and wades across to Ireland with his host. The Irish fall back across a river and break the bridge, but Bendigeidfran lies down as a bridge himself; Matholwch then offers the kingship to Gwern, and builds a house big enough to hold Bendigeidfran. The Irish hide armed men in hide bags on its pillars, but Efnysien finds them and crushes their heads one by one, and sings an englyn over the last; then the two hosts sit down together and the kingship is conferred on the boy.
